hints: Compare the electrons in the two half-equations. One gains $6\text{e}^-$ and the other loses $2\text{e}^-$, so think what multiplier will make the electrons equal.
Multiply the oxidation half-equation to match electrons, then add the two equations and cancel $\text{e}^-$ and any excess $\text{H}^+$ on both sides.
walkthrough:
Balance the electrons first**
Think of electrons as the currency of redox. The dichromate half-equation needs $6\text{e}^-$: $$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The ethanedioic acid half-equation only supplies $2\text{e}^-$: $$\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^-$$ To make them match, multiply the whole second equation by $3$.

Add and simplify**
After multiplying you have: $$3\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^-$$ Now add to the reduction equation. The $6\text{e}^-$ cancel exactly. You have $14\text{H}^+$ on the left and $6\text{H}^+$ on the right, leaving $8\text{H}^+$ on the left. That gives the overall ionic equation: $$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 8\text{H}^+ + 3\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{CO}_2 + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and charge balance to be safe.

hints: Start from $n = c \times V$ and remember to convert the volume from $\text{cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$ by dividing by $1000$.
walkthrough:
Convert volume and multiply**
For any solution, amount is concentration times volume in $\text{dm}^3$: $$n = c \times V$$ Here $V = 32.0 \text{ cm}^3 = \frac{32.0}{1000} = 0.0320 \text{ dm}^3$. So: $$n = 0.0200 \times 0.0320 = 6.40 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$ This is the amount of dichromate that reacted.

hints: Look back at your overall equation in (a) to find how many moles of $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ react with $1$ mole of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$.
walkthrough:
Use the 1 to 3 ratio**
Your equation in (a) shows: $$1\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} : 3\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$$ So every mole of dichromate oxidises three moles of ethanedioic acid. Multiply: $$n(\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4) = 3 \times 6.40 \times 10^{-4} = 1.92 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$

hints: You know the mass of the hydrated sample ($0.242 \text{ g}$) and the moles of $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ it contains. Recall how $M_r$ links mass and moles.
walkthrough:
Divide mass by moles**
The $1.92 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$ you found is the amount of hydrated acid in the $0.242 \text{ g}$ sample, because each formula unit $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4.x\text{H}_2\text{O}$ contains one $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$. Use: $$M_r = \frac{m}{n}$$ $$M_r = \frac{0.242}{1.92 \times 10^{-3}} = 126.0$$ No units for $M_r$, it is a relative mass.

hints: Calculate $M_r$ of anhydrous $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ (about $90$) and subtract it from $126.0$ to leave the mass due to water, then divide by $18.0$.
walkthrough:
Separate the water mass**
First work out the anhydrous part: $$M_r(\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4) = (2 \times 1.0) + (2 \times 12.0) + (4 \times 16.0) = 90.0$$ Your hydrated $M_r$ is $126.0$, so the difference must be water: $$126.0 - 90.0 = 36.0$$ Since $M_r(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 18.0$: $$x = \frac{36.0}{18.0} = 2$$ The formula is $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4.2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
